<explanation>
This project is CSharpier, an opinionated code formatter for C#. It’s essentially a developer tool that leverages Roslyn to parse and “pretty-print” C# code using a set of well-defined rules. When designing the system diagram for this project, you will want to capture both the core formatting engine and the various ways that it integrates with external environments (CLI, IDE integrations, build tools, website playground, etc.). Below are detailed steps and guidelines tailored to CSharpier’s architecture:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Core Formatting Engine – This is the backbone of CSharpier and includes components responsible for parsing C# code (using Roslyn), generating the syntax, applying formatting rules, and then printing the formatted output. It’s represented by modules like “CSharpier”, “CodeFormatter”, “DocPrinter”, “SyntaxPrinter”, and related utility classes.
   • CLI Application – Found in Src/CSharpier.Cli and its tests (Src/CSharpier.Cli.Tests). This component provides a command-line interface where a user can invoke “dotnet csharpier” to format code.
   • Integration/Extension Projects – These include components for editor integrations such as Visual Studio (Src/CSharpier.VisualStudio), Rider (Src/CSharpier.Rider), and VSCode, as well as integration with MsBuild (Src/CSharpier.MsBuild) and possibly other build tools.
   • Playground & Website – The Playground (Src/CSharpier.Playground) and Website (Src/Website) provide user interfaces (often web-based) for demo purposes, documentation, and an online “try-it-out” experience.
   • Testing and Code Generation – There are dedicated test projects (in Tests and various Src/CSharpier.Tests directories) as well as generators (e.g., Src/CSharpier.Generators, Src/CSharpier.FakeGenerators) which help validate the formatting rules.
   • Build and Infrastructure Scripts – The repository also includes various CI/CD workflows, configuration files (e.g., .github/workflows), Dockerfiles, and helper scripts (in Shell and Scripts directories) which orchestrate automated testing, publishing, and deployment.

2. Determine Relationships and Interactions:
   • The CLI and Integration projects consume the core formatting engine to actually perform the code formatting. Your diagram should show how the CLI (and other application layers) calls into the formatting libraries.
   • The Playground and Website interact with both the core services and potentially the CLI interfaces in a client-server or web service-like pattern to provide a live demonstration of the formatting.
   • Testing components are connected to the core engine and CLI components, ensuring that changes in the formatting logic trigger comprehensive automated tests.
   • Code generators and tools (from the Generators folders) interface with the core library or help update/reinforce the compatibility between new Roslyn features and the tool’s formatting output.
   • The CI/CD and build scripts (GitHub workflows, Dockerfiles, shell scripts) interact with all the above components to build, test, and deploy the tool and its extensions.

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modularity and Separation of Concerns: The project is structured into separate solutions, projects, and libraries to decouple the engine from the different integration points.
   • Reusability: The core formatting library is reused across the CLI, integration projects, and even for generating formatted documentation on the website.
   • Automated Testing and CI: Multiple test suites (including integration tests, end-to-end tests, and formatting tests) help ensure the tool maintains a consistent output.
   • Consistent Configuration Management: Use of Directory.Build.props/Directory.Packages.props and centralized configuration across the solution that helps maintain consistent dependency versions and build settings.

4. Incorporate Relevant Technologies and Frameworks:
   • .NET / C# and Roslyn – The primary platform and language; Roslyn is the parsing and code analysis engine.
   • Prettier-inspired Printing Engine – While the printing process is evolved from the original prettier, it has been adapted to cater to C# formatting rules.
   • Docker, GitHub Actions, and MSBuild – Employed for CI/CD, testing, packaging, and deployment.
   • Web Technologies – In the Website and Playground (e.g., use of Docusaurus for documentation and modern front-end frameworks in ClientApp).

5. Tailor the Diagram for This Developer Tool:
   • Emphasize the separation between the “core formatting engine” and its various consumers (CLI, IDE integrations, website).
   • Draw distinct sections for the core libraries, testing infrastructure, and integration endpoints.
   • If desired, map out the flow of code: Input source code → Parsing (via Roslyn) → Formatting (Rules & Printer modules) → Output formatted code. Then show how different consumers (CLI, extensions, playground) use that same pipeline.
   • If space permits, include build and deployment automation segments (CI/CD workflows, Docker deployments) to showcase the end-to-end process.

6. Guidelines for the Diagram’s Visual Elements:
   • Use clear, descriptive labels for each major component (e.g., “Core Formatting Engine”, “CLI Client”, “Visual Studio Integration”, “Website Playground”, “Test Suite”).
   • Utilize directional arrows to show how data flows between these components. For example, arrows from the CLI to the Core Engine, or from the Core Engine to the Test Suite.
   • Apply color coding or use distinct shapes: you might use one color for core libraries, another for integration tools, and different icons for build/deployment scripts versus end-user applications.
   • Consider grouping related components within boundaries (e.g., a bordered area for “Editor Integrations” that contains Visual Studio, Rider, and VSCode-related projects).

7. Final Detailed Diagram Instruction:
   • Identify and list each major project segment as nodes.
   • Draw interconnecting arrows where, for instance, the CLI, MsBuild, and Editor Integrations all depend on the central Core Formatting Engine.
   • Represent the testing framework and CI/CD pipelines as peripheral but connected elements that serve all modules.
   • Ensure that the website/playground is depicted as both a consumer and a showcase of the formatting capabilities.
   • Highlight external dependencies like Roslyn and .NET Core, as well as community integrations (e.g., Discord for community engagement, GitHub workflows for deployment).

By capturing these components and interactions in your diagram, you’ll provide a comprehensive, detailed view of CSharpier’s architecture. This visualization will help current developers, contributors, and integrators quickly understand the overall structure and the specific responsibilities of each component in the system.
</explanation>
